titre: The ILO Never Promised Equal Work, but Work of Equal Value
accroche: The ILO's equal remuneration convention does not say equal work, but work of equal value. The nuance changes what it can correct.
contenu_vulgarise:
Geneva, June 29, 1951. Meeting for its thirty-fourth session, the International Labour Conference adopts Convention No. 100 of the International Labour Organization, devoted to equal remuneration for men and women workers. At first glance, the principle seems perfectly simple: equal work, equal pay. That is not, however, the formula the text adopts. Its first article defines the principle as equal remuneration "for work of equal value," and this choice of words, far from a stylistic variant, changes what the convention can actually correct.

## A Word That Changes What Can Be Compared

"Equal work, equal pay" applies only to two people holding, in the same business, an identical or nearly identical position. The formula the convention adopts, "work of equal value," also allows different jobs to be compared, as long as an objective evaluation shows they are worth the same. The International Labour Organization itself gives examples of comparisons made on this basis: cooks and cleaners, female-dominated occupations, compared with gardeners and drivers, male-dominated; social affairs managers compared with engineers; flight attendants compared with pilots and mechanics. Article 3 of the convention provides precisely this route: members must promote the objective appraisal of jobs on the basis of the work they involve, that is, the qualification required, the effort, the responsibilities, in order to set pay without reference to the sex of the person holding the job.

This distinction matters because the pay gap between men and women rarely comes from paying two people in the same position differently, a practice too visible to last without being challenged. It comes from occupational segregation: the occupations where women are the majority are, on average and at comparable qualification, paid less than those where men are. A rule limited to "equal work" can do nothing about that gap, since no one there holds the same position as a person of the other sex. A rule based on "equal value" can, at least in principle, by setting side by side occupations that nothing, at first glance, brings together.

## A Principle Laid Down, an Evaluation Still to Be Done

The convention does not say how to evaluate the value of a job: it leaves this to each member, through law, classification grids, or collective bargaining. The principle laid down in 1951 therefore does not apply by itself; it depends entirely on the method each country chooses to compare jobs that, on paper, do not resemble each other. The difference between the two formulas, equal work and work of equal value, remains largely unknown outside labor law, even though it separates a rule with almost no reach from one that can genuinely bite into the pay gap between female-dominated and male-dominated occupations.

repere.texte: the term equal remuneration for men and women workers for work of equal value refers to rates of remuneration established without discrimination based on sex.
repere.source: Equal Remuneration Convention, 1951 (No. 100), Article 1, paragraph (b), International Labour Organization

carte.punch: The 1951 convention does not say equal work, it says work of equal value
carte.idee: Convention No. 100 of the International Labour Organization, adopted in 1951, does not require equal pay for identical work, but for work of equal value, a formula that allows different occupations to be compared and not only two strictly similar positions.

quiz.question: Why is the formula adopted by ILO Convention No. 100, "work of equal value," broader than "equal work"?
choix: Because it imposes a single minimum wage, identical in all countries that ratify the convention
Because it also applies to comparisons between different occupations, as long as an objective evaluation shows comparable value
Because it applies only to public-sector jobs, excluding private businesses
Because it replaces pay with a points system assigned to each task performed
quiz.explication: "Equal work" compares only two identical positions held by a man and a woman in the same business. "Work of equal value" allows different occupations to be compared, for example flight attendants and pilots, on the basis of objective criteria such as qualification, effort, and responsibility.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Article 3 of Convention No. 100 provide for comparing different occupations?
choix: A single minimum wage set by the International Labour Organization
An objective appraisal of jobs according to qualification, effort, and responsibilities
A mandatory quota of women in each occupational category
An individual negotiation between each employee and their employer
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Article 3 encourages the objective appraisal of jobs on the basis of the work to be performed, without reference to the sex of the person holding them.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What example of a comparison between occupations does the International Labour Organization give to illustrate work of equal value?
choix: Flight attendants compared with pilots and mechanics
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The ILO cites in particular the comparison between flight attendants, a female-dominated occupation, and pilots and mechanics, male-dominated.
